find: Enid speaks predominantly in standard English — the language of assimilation. She has deliberately cultivated a 'respectable' way of speaking that signals her integration into English society. But when she is emotional, stressed or speaking about Jamaica, her language shifts: Jamaican patois breaks through the English surface. These moments of linguistic slippage are dramatically powerful because they reveal the Caribbean identity Enid has worked so hard to suppress.
replace: Enid speaks Jamaican patois all through the play, even while she preaches assimilation to her daughters: 'I proud a my girls', 'England been good to me'. Her voice never becomes English, however hard she pushes English respectability on Del and Viv. That contradiction is dramatically powerful: the audience hears the Jamaica she tells her daughters to leave behind.
note: F3: Enid speaks Jamaican patois throughout; she does not speak standard English with occasional slippage

find: Enid code-switches unconsciously when her emotional defences are down — her patois emerging under pressure. Mai speaks with a stronger Jamaican register throughout, reflecting her uncompromised connection to Caribbean culture.
replace: Enid and Mai both speak Jamaican patois, and Mai's register is the richest — proverbial, rhythmic and rooted in Jamaican oral tradition. Enid's patois carries her past even while she argues for English respectability.

find: And it is dramatic: when Enid's patois breaks through, the audience hears the identity she has been suppressing.
replace: And it is dramatic: when Enid argues for English respectability in Jamaican patois, the audience hears the contradiction she is living.

find: Enid's adoption of it is a conscious choice to be taken seriously in a society that marginalises Caribbean speakers. But the play shows that this choice has a cost: in gaining English respectability, Enid has lost the linguistic connection to her heritage.
replace: Enid pushes it on her daughters so that they will be taken seriously in a society that marginalises Caribbean speakers. But the play shows the cost: her daughters gain the accent she wanted for them, and lose the language that ties them to Jamaica.

find: Enid's language sits between Jamaica and England.
replace: Enid's language is Jamaican throughout, even though her ambitions for her daughters are English.

find: This generational progression — from patois-inflected English (Enid) to fully English (Viv) to consciously reclaiming patois (Del) — mirrors the broader pattern of immigrant linguistic experience. The first generation compromises; the second generation assimilates; the third generation often seeks to reconnect with the language their grandparents spoke.
replace: This progression — from Jamaican patois (Enid) to fully English (Viv) to Del, drawn back towards Jamaican speech through Mai — mirrors the broader pattern of immigrant linguistic experience. The first generation keeps its language; the next assimilates; then some reach back for what was lost.

find: When Enid corrects Del's speech or insists on 'proper' English, she is performing her assimilation strategy through language.
replace: When Enid insists on 'proper' English for her daughters, she is enforcing an assimilation strategy she does not follow in her own speech.
